description:
Longitudinal archive of the chainsaw suites' published diagnostics grammar in ppat/homelab-ops-kubernetes-apps -- READY, MODE, PULL, CONTENTION, RESTART, UNCENSORED -- kept past the 90 days GitHub retains job logs. Fed by the ci-diagnostics CronJob, which pulls from the GitHub Actions API. Nothing is pushed from CI; there is no inbound path.

BUILT FOR THEN, NOT FOR NOW. Every panel here is a weekly or 28-day aggregate, because the questions this archive exists to answer get asked in six months. Set the range to straddle a change and read across it. The four rows are the four questions, in the order someone reaches for them: did my change help; when did it start getting worse and what moved; what is about to break; and can I trust a comparison across this range at all.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. Per-run detail and raw line dumps. Explore does that better -- start from `{job="ci-diagnostics"}` and filter by `suite` and `instrument`. A panel that reproduces Explore badly is worse than a link.

THE THREE THINGS MOST LIKELY TO MISLEAD YOU. **A young series looks broken** -- a few hours of data on a 90-day axis is a hairline at the right edge; narrow the range. **Population** -- `schedule` is the controlled sample and everything else is contaminated by whatever the branch changed. **Comparability** -- the warning stat at the top is a weak proxy until `cpu_model` lands (apps#3751); a comparison spanning a runner hardware change is invalid and nothing here can currently prove it did not.

Deliberately no alert rules, per the standing no-alerting-until-AI-triage doctrine. The liveness stats at the top are the detection mechanism, not a backstop to one.

panels.title: Can this page be believed right now? (ignores every filter)

panels.description:
One OUTCOME entry per (run, attempt, job). Read this first: every panel below renders empty when the ingester has stopped, and an empty CI dashboard looks exactly like a quiet fleet.

Healthy floor is ~64 even with no PR activity -- 16 suites sampled four times a day. Zero means the CronJob in the ci-diagnostics namespace has not written; check `kubectl -n ci-diagnostics get cronjob ci-diagnostics` and its last Job's logs.
panels.title: Jobs ingested, last 24h

panels.description:
Distinct `suite` values in the OUTCOME stream. Catches what a count cannot: a pass that died halfway leaves a healthy-looking total with some suites silently missing, and a per-suite chart drawn over that shows a gap that reads as 'this suite did not run'.

16-17 is healthy. A number that drops and stays down is the signal, not any single reading.
panels.title: Suites seen, last 24h

panels.description:
**A comparability warning, not a health metric.** Distinct `nproc` values across CONTENTION lines. More than one means the range you are looking at spans more than one runner shape, and a before/after drawn across it is comparing different machines as well as different code.

It is a **weak** proxy and deliberately labelled as one: it cannot see a host swap that kept the same core count, which is the likeliest kind. `cpu_model` is the field that actually settles this and it lands with apps#3751 -- until then this stat is the best available and is not sufficient.

Deliberately NOT built on `calib_ms`, which looks like the obvious CPU proxy: it is a relative index tied to a fixed iteration count, so editing that count silently rebases the whole historical series. Harmless over a week, fatal over the year this archive covers.
panels.title: Runner configurations seen in the last 30d

panels.description:
OUTCOME entries on **successful** runs whose diagnostics were incomplete -- `no-lines` or `partial`. The verdict is a necessary-consequence test: a healthy run must leave a `CONTENTION start`, a `CONTENTION end` and at least one `READY`.

Restricted to successes on purpose. A run that fails before anything becomes Ready legitimately emits no READY, so counting failures here would light this up on ordinary red runs and make the one indicator the page depends on into noise. `assertion-semantics` is excluded by name: it pins chainsaw's assertion semantics rather than deploying a module, so it emits none of the grammar by design.

targets.expr: sum(count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite!="assertion-semantics"} | outcome = "success" | instrumentation =~ "no-lines|partial" [24h])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Jobs with broken instrumentation, 24h
1. I changed something -- did it help?

panels.description:
`pull_s` is the kubelet's own pull duration; `incl_wait_s` adds time queued behind the kubelet's serial pull queue (`serializeImagePulls: true` in the kind node image).

**The gap between the two lines is the entire multi-node and parallel-pull argument.** Extra kind nodes add no CPU; what they add is a second kubelet pull queue. A change that helps shows the upper line falling toward the lower one while the lower barely moves.

Read that asymmetry deliberately, because the obvious reading is wrong: with parallel pulls enabled, individual pulls get *slower* under contention while the set finishes earlier, so `pull_s` alone reads like a regression when the change was an improvement. Judge on `incl_wait_s`.

Weekly quantile, not trailing-day: at four scheduled runs per suite per day a daily p90 is mostly noise, and this panel exists to be read across months.

The `by ()` is load-bearing -- structured metadata is part of a series' identity, so without an explicit grouping LogQL computes the quantile per entry over a single sample and returns that sample, which an outer `avg()` then averages into a mean. Measured on this instance the two forms differ by 2.9x.

Cannot see: images already cached emit PULL-CACHED and no PULL line, so a week with more caching shows fewer pulls, not faster ones.

defaults.noValue: No PULL lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="pull", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap incl_wait_s [7d]) by ()
quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="pull", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap pull_s [7d]) by ()

panels.title: Image pull cost, weekly p90: queue wait vs kubelet pull

panels.description:
How long the shared prerequisite phase took, per suite: the `T0+` offset at which `kustomization/flux-system/pre-requisites` became Ready.

This is the phase the fixture work was aimed at -- removing external-secrets' `dependsOn: cert-manager-release` -- so it is where that change should show up. It is also the dominant cost in most suites.

**A caveat that limits what this can be compared against.** `T0` is the earliest transition in that run's own list, not the suite's start. So these offsets are comparable *between runs of the same suite* and are **not** subtractable from job duration or from the chainsaw phase. That is why the decomposition panel below plots the three phases separately instead of stacking them.

Median rather than p90: this phase is bimodal, so a high quantile mostly reports which mode won rather than how long the phase took. The mode split itself is the panel below.

defaults.noValue: No prerequisite READY lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.5, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | name="pre-requisites" | kind="kustomization" | unwrap t0_s [7d]) by (suite)

panels.title: Prerequisite phase duration, weekly median by suite

panels.description:
`ctrl_webhook_gap_s` from every MODE line, bucketed into a density map: one column per day, 5-second rows, colour is how many runs landed in that band.

**This is the sharpest fact in the dataset and the panel exists to falsify it.** The claim is that the gap is bimodal -- roughly 20-26s or 75-97s, with *zero* intermediates across every run ever classified -- and that no resource story can produce that, because contention gives continua and heavy tails rather than two clean bands with an empty gulf between them.

A scatter shows you the points; only a density map shows you whether the **bands themselves are moving**, whether the slow band is getting heavier, and whether the empty middle ever fills in. Over months that is the whole question.

**If the middle fills in, the quantizer argument is dead** and the slow-mode explanation needs rebuilding. That is the single observation most worth watching here.

One caveat on the reducer. LogQL has no histogram, so this is `max_over_time` over the panel's own step and Grafana buckets the values. The scheduled fleet runs a suite every six hours, so at day-width columns a bucket holds at most a handful of runs per suite and each contributes one value. Colliding samples would show only the larger -- which can hide a fast run but cannot manufacture an intermediate one, so it cannot produce a false refutation.

`mode=none` runs are excluded: they carry `ctrl_webhook_gap_s=-`, which is not a measurement.

targets.expr: max_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="mode", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | mode != "none" | ctrl_webhook_gap_s != "-" | unwrap ctrl_webhook_gap_s [$__interval]) by (suite)

panels.title: Controller -> webhook gap, density over time

panels.description:
Every run emits one MODE line classifying the external-secrets controller -> its own webhook gap. Published bands: `fast` <= 35s, `slow` >= 60s, `intermediate` is the 36-59s band, `none` means the suite has no external-secrets fixture or the pods never became Ready.

**Stacked as counts, not percentages, and that is load-bearing.** On a percentage axis '0% slow' and 'no runs at all' draw identically. With counts the total height is the run count, so a quiet week is visibly short rather than invisibly clean.

A mean is not available and would be wrong if it were: the underlying gap is bimodal, so an average sits in a region no run has ever occupied and drifts smoothly when what actually changed is a ratio.

**Watch for `intermediate`.** No run has ever produced one. Its appearance would falsify the quantizer explanation the whole slow-mode analysis rests on, so it is left in the query rather than filtered away as a permanently empty series.

defaults.noValue: No MODE lines in range. Note these only exist on runs after apps#3738 landed.

panels.title: Prerequisite mode, weekly run counts
2. It got worse -- when did it start, and what moved?

panels.description:
`prerequisite`, `chainsaw` and `job` are nested in reality -- prerequisite is inside the chainsaw phase, which is inside the job -- and the obvious chart is a stacked one showing where a regression lives.

**That chart cannot be built from this data and this one is deliberately not it.** The prerequisite figure is a `T0+` offset, where `T0` is the earliest Ready transition in that run's own list; the chainsaw figure is `elapsed_s` measured from the suite's actual start; the job figure is GitHub's wall clock. Three different origins. Subtracting or stacking them produces a number that means nothing, and LogQL cannot join streams to reconcile them.

So read these as **three independent trends on a shared time axis**: if the job line rises and the chainsaw line does not, the regression is in fixed overhead (checkout, `kind create`, `flux install`); if chainsaw rises with prerequisite flat, it is in the validates. That inference is sound. Reading a gap between the lines as a duration is not.

A true decomposition is possible but needs the ingester to compute it: `READY` carries absolute `ready_at` timestamps, so the phase boundaries can be derived at write time. Until then this panel is the honest version.

defaults.noValue: No phase data in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.5, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | name="pre-requisites" | kind="kustomization" | unwrap t0_s [7d]) by ()
quantile_over_time(0.5, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | boundary="end" | unwrap elapsed_s [7d]) by ()

quantile_over_time(0.5, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome="success" | duration_s != "" | unwrap duration_s [7d]) by ()

panels.title: The three phases, weekly median -- NOT a decomposition

panels.description:
`READY` is the richest line in the grammar -- one entry per pod, Kustomization and HelmRelease, with the `T0+` offset at which it became Ready -- and it is what actually answers *what moved*. When the phase panel beside this one shows a rise, this says which component caused it.

Grouped by `kind` and `namespace` rather than by object name, deliberately: pod names carry two random suffixes, so grouping by name would mint a new series per run and blow `max_query_series`. Namespace is the stable proxy for 'component'.

This is the earliest available signal that a chart bump slowed something down -- it moves before a budget expires and long before anything goes red.

Same `T0` caveat as everywhere else: offsets are comparable between runs of a suite, not against job duration. Narrow `suite` to one value before reading absolute numbers.

defaults.noValue: No READY lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap t0_s [7d]) by (kind, namespace)

panels.title: Time-to-ready by component, weekly p90

panels.description:
Non-success OUTCOME entries over all OUTCOME entries, per suite, on a 28-day rolling window.

**This was cut from an earlier version of this dashboard and is deliberately back.** Cutting it was right for a 28-day view of a young series and wrong for the horizon this archive exists to serve: at four scheduled runs per suite per day, a month is n=112 and a year is n>1400. The first cannot resolve a change anyone would act on; the second resolves plenty.

**`ci/scripts/baseline-census.sh` remains authoritative for exact rates.** It reads job metadata, which outlives logs indefinitely, and it classifies ceiling kills properly -- GitHub reports a `timeout-minutes` kill as `cancelled`, identically to a concurrency cancel. This panel's value is not precision, it is being on the same time axis as pull cost, mode share and contention, so an inflection can be lined up across all of them.

`outcome` here is the discriminated field, not the raw conclusion, so `timed_out` and `superseded` are separable. **`superseded` counts as a failure**, which overstates the rate on busy PR days -- filter the population to `schedule` to remove that entirely.

defaults.noValue: No OUTCOME samples in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome != "success" [28d])) / sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" [28d]))

panels.title: Failure rate by suite, rolling 28d
3. What is about to break?

panels.description:
`READY` records each object's Ready condition at report time. This counts the ones that were **not** `True` on runs that nevertheless **succeeded**.

**This is the primary at-risk signal on this page, and it is better than anything failures can give you, because it fires before anything fails.** `Ready: Unknown` means the controller had not yet reconciled that object when the suite finished asserting -- the run passed on timing it did not have much of. A real example already in the data: `apps-ai`, a successful scheduled run, `kustomization/flux-system/pre-requisites` at `Ready: Unknown` with `t0_s=424`.

The discriminator this rests on is recorded elsewhere in this project: **`Ready: Unknown` means under-budgeted; `Ready: False` with a reason means broken.** A rising count here is a suite drifting toward its budget while still green.

Contrast with the UNCENSORED panel beside it, which is post-hoc by construction: it can only tell you about assertions that already expired. This one is the leading indicator and that one is the trailing one.

defaults.noValue: Nothing was Unknown on a passing run in this range -- which on this panel is good news, provided the liveness stats at the top are non-zero.

targets.expr: sum by (suite, kind) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome="success" | ready_state != "True" [7d]))

panels.title: Objects that were still Unknown when a run PASSED, weekly

panels.description:
`UNCENSORED` exists on **failing runs only** and is the answer to a question nothing else can reach: every timeout failure is censored at its own budget, so an assert dying at 60.0s of a 60s budget tells you nothing about what it needed. After a suite goes red a watch keeps observing and records how much longer each not-Ready object actually took.

Ranked by `extra_s` rather than dumped chronologically, because the useful question is *which objects need the most headroom*, not *what failed last Tuesday*. The top rows are where a budget is most wrong. **Prefer this number over any multiplier when sizing a budget** -- it reports what the step actually needed.

What it cannot tell you: the grammar records **objects**, not step names, and carries no budgets at all -- those live in the suite YAML. So this ranks *what needed time*, not *which assertion is closest to expiring*. The panel to its left is the closer thing to the latter.

`never` on a CNPG Cluster is a real bug (#3678), not an under-sized budget. And these live overwhelmingly on PR runs, so the population filter does not reach this panel -- filtering it would leave it empty on almost every visit, and empty would read as 'nothing needed extra time'.

targets.expr: topk(20, max by (suite, kind, namespace, name) (max_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="uncensored", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | extra_s != "" | unwrap extra_s [$__range])))

panels.title: What failing steps actually needed, ranked by extra time

panels.description:
`RESTART` records containers that crashed and recovered **inside** an assertion's budget -- invisible everywhere else, because the suite still passes and the pod still reports Ready.

This is not a curiosity. This estate deliberately tolerates longhorn's crash-restart cycle, and the stated reason that tolerance is safe is that restart counts stay visible on green runs. **If restarts creep up, a regression is hiding inside a passing suite and this is the only panel that would show it.**

Grouped by container rather than pod: pod names carry random suffixes and would mint a new series per run.

Read the shape, not the level. A steady background from a known-flappy component is the expected state; a new container appearing, or an existing one stepping up, is the finding.

defaults.noValue: No RESTART lines in range -- no container crashed inside an assertion budget.

targets.expr: sum by (container) (sum_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="restart", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | container != "" | unwrap restarts [7d]))

panels.title: Container restarts inside a run, weekly total
4. Can I trust a comparison across this range?

panels.description:
Two CONTENTION probes per run -- one at the start of the chainsaw phase, one at the end -- never in between, because a bandwidth probe fired mid-run would *be* the contention it claims to measure.

`net_mbps` is drawn as its weekly **10th percentile**: bandwidth is the axis measured to matter (a 150mbit shaped link reproduced the failures 6/6 on the rig, while halving cluster CPU changed nothing), and what hurts is the floor dropping, not the mean. `fsync_us` is drawn as its weekly **p90** and is present for elimination rather than as an established cause -- it is the untested candidate for the prerequisite phase's bimodality.

Use this to qualify the panels above: a week where the bandwidth floor collapsed is a week whose pull times mean something different. It does **not** tell you the runs are otherwise comparable -- that is what the warning stat at the top of the page is for, and it is currently weak.

`calib_ms` is deliberately absent from this page entirely. It is a relative index tied to a fixed iteration count, so editing that count silently rebases the whole series -- a step change indistinguishable from a real one, which is exactly what a months-long archive cannot survive.

defaults.noValue: No CONTENTION lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.1, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | net_mbps =~ "[0-9].*" | unwrap net_mbps [7d]) by ()
quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | fsync_us =~ "[0-9].*" | unwrap fsync_us [7d]) by ()

list.description: Which Loki to read. The value is the datasource UID, not its display name.
list.label: Datasource
list.name: datasource

list.description:
Which chainsaw suites to include. Reaches every panel except the liveness stats at the top and the UNCENSORED ranking, which deliberately ignore it.

What makes All safe is `allValue: .*`, not the anchoring -- the two pull opposite ways. An empty selection matches nothing (`^()$` matches only the empty string) and renders an empty page rather than an error. If everything is blank, check this before concluding the ingester stopped.
list.label: Suite
list.name: suite

list.description:
Which population of runs to read. **The most consequential control here.**

`schedule` is the designed sample: sixteen suites, four fixed slots a day, always `main`, with suite content that only changes when someone merges. It is the only population in which a before/after means anything.

`pull_request` runs execute arbitrary branch code -- a PR that changes a suite's budgets or node count moves the very numbers being trended -- and `push` runs are path-filtered, so a suite is sampled more often precisely when it is being worked on. Pooling either into a trend is the contaminated measurement this series exists to replace.

It deliberately does not reach the UNCENSORED ranking, which lives almost entirely on PR failures and would be empty on nearly every visit.
list.label: Population
list.name: population
